title: MCAT: Physics Formulas
description: For MCAT learners reviewing mechanics, fluids, thermodynamics, electricity, waves, optics, and atomic physics. Equations include assumptions and symbol meanings; verify with current guidelines for exam scope.

cards.front: What is average velocity?
cards.back: v_avg = Δx/Δt. Displacement Δx is signed; Δt is elapsed time. SI unit: m/s.

cards.front: What is average speed?
cards.back: Average speed = total distance/elapsed time. Unlike velocity, speed has no direction.

cards.front: What is average acceleration?
cards.back: a_avg = Δv/Δt, where v is velocity. SI unit: m/s².

cards.front: For constant acceleration, how does velocity change with time?
cards.back: v = v0 + at, where v0 is initial velocity and a is constant acceleration.

cards.front: For constant acceleration, what is displacement after time t?
cards.back: Δx = v0t + (1/2)at² along the chosen axis.

cards.front: Which constant-acceleration equation eliminates time?
cards.back: v² = v0² + 2aΔx.

cards.front: What is average velocity under constant acceleration?
cards.back: v_avg = (v0 + v)/2 along a fixed axis.

cards.front: How do you resolve initial projectile velocity at angle θ above horizontal?
cards.back: v0x = v0 cos θ; v0y = v0 sin θ.

cards.front: What is horizontal projectile displacement without air resistance?
cards.back: Δx = v0 cos θ × t, assuming no horizontal acceleration.

cards.front: What is vertical projectile displacement without air resistance?
cards.back: Δy = v0 sin θ × t − (1/2)gt², taking upward as positive.

cards.front: What is projectile flight time for equal launch and landing heights?
cards.back: T = 2v0 sin θ/g, neglecting air resistance.

cards.front: What is projectile range for equal launch and landing heights?
cards.back: R = v0² sin(2θ)/g, neglecting air resistance.

cards.front: What is maximum rise above launch height for a projectile?
cards.back: H = v0² sin²θ/(2g), neglecting air resistance.

cards.front: What is Newton's second law for constant mass?
cards.back: ΣF = ma. Net force and acceleration are vectors.

cards.front: What is weight near Earth's surface?
cards.back: W = mg, downward; g is approximately 9.8 m/s² near the surface.

cards.front: What is kinetic friction in the simple dry-friction model?
cards.back: f_k = μ_k N, opposite relative sliding. N is normal force; μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction.

cards.front: What inequality describes static friction?
cards.back: 0 ≤ f_s ≤ μ_s N. Static friction adjusts to prevent slipping, up to its maximum.

cards.front: What is the normal force on a frictionless incline with no other perpendicular forces?
cards.back: N = mg cos θ, where θ is the incline angle above horizontal.

cards.front: What gravitational force component points down an incline?
cards.back: F_parallel = mg sin θ, where θ is the incline angle above horizontal.

cards.front: What is Hooke's law for an ideal spring?
cards.back: F_s = −kx, where x is displacement from equilibrium and k is spring stiffness.

cards.front: What is centripetal acceleration?
cards.back: a_c = v²/r = ω²r, directed toward the center of a circular path.

cards.front: What net radial force is required for circular motion?
cards.back: ΣF_radial = mv²/r = mω²r, toward the center. This is not an additional force type.

cards.front: How are tangential speed and angular speed related?
cards.back: v = rω, with ω in radians per second.

cards.front: What is angular speed in terms of period?
cards.back: ω = 2π/T = 2πf, where T is period and f is frequency.

cards.front: What is torque magnitude?
cards.back: τ = rF sin θ = F times the perpendicular lever arm; θ is the angle between r and F.

cards.front: What conditions define static mechanical equilibrium?
cards.back: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. The object has neither linear nor angular acceleration.

cards.front: What is the center of mass of point masses along x?
cards.back: x_cm = Σ(m_i x_i)/Σm_i.

cards.front: What is work by a constant force?
cards.back: W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

cards.front: What is the work-energy theorem?
cards.back: W_net = ΔK. Net work equals change in kinetic energy.

cards.front: What is translational kinetic energy?
What is change in gravitational potential energy near Earth?
cards.back: ΔU_g = mgΔh, with approximately constant g.

cards.front: What is elastic potential energy in an ideal spring?
cards.back: U_s = (1/2)kx², measured relative to the unstretched equilibrium position.

cards.front: When is mechanical energy conserved?
cards.back: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f when only conservative forces do work.

cards.front: How does nonconservative work change mechanical energy?
cards.back: W_nc = Δ(K + U), for a system whose conservative forces are represented by U.

cards.front: What is average power?
cards.back: P_avg = W/Δt. SI unit: watt, or joule per second.

cards.front: What is instantaneous mechanical power for a force?
cards.back: P = F · v = Fv cos θ.

cards.front: What is linear momentum?
cards.back: p = mv for nonrelativistic motion; momentum is a vector.

cards.front: What is impulse?
cards.back: J = ∫F dt = Δp. For constant force, J = FΔt.

cards.front: When is total linear momentum conserved?
cards.back: Σp_initial = Σp_final when the net external impulse is zero.

cards.front: What is conserved in an elastic collision?
cards.back: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved for an isolated system.

cards.front: What is the final velocity after a perfectly inelastic one-dimensional collision?
cards.back: v_f = (m1v1 + m2v2)/(m1 + m2), when the objects stick and external impulse is negligible.

cards.front: What is Newton's law of gravitation?
cards.back: F = Gm1m2/r², where r is center-to-center separation for point masses or nonoverlapping spherical masses.

cards.front: What is gravitational field magnitude outside a spherical mass?
cards.back: g = GM/r², where r is distance from its center.

cards.front: What is gravitational potential energy for two point masses?
cards.back: U = −GMm/r, taking U = 0 at infinite separation.

cards.front: What is circular orbital speed about a much heavier mass?
cards.back: v = √(GM/r), where r is orbital radius and M is the central mass.

cards.front: What is escape speed from radius r about mass M?
cards.back: v_esc = √(2GM/r), neglecting drag and other masses.

cards.front: What is density?
cards.back: ρ = m/V. SI unit: kg/m³.

cards.front: What is pressure?
cards.back: P = F_perpendicular/A. SI unit: pascal, or N/m².

cards.front: What is hydrostatic gauge pressure at depth h?
cards.back: P_gauge = ρgh for a constant-density fluid at rest.

cards.front: How are absolute and gauge pressure related?
cards.back: P_absolute = P_gauge + P_atmospheric.

cards.front: What is the buoyant force?
cards.back: F_b = ρ_fluid V_displaced g, equal to the weight of displaced fluid.

cards.front: What fraction of a floating object's volume is submerged?
cards.back: V_sub/V_total = ρ_object/ρ_fluid for a uniformly dense object floating at rest.

cards.front: What is the volume flow rate through a pipe?
cards.back: Q = Av, where v is the cross-sectional average speed.

cards.front: What is continuity for steady incompressible flow?
cards.back: A1v1 = A2v2. Volume flow rate is constant along an unbranched stream tube.

cards.front: What is Bernoulli's equation in ideal flow?
cards.back: P + (1/2)ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline for steady, incompressible, nonviscous flow.

cards.front: What is Poiseuille's law for laminar pipe flow?
cards.back: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), for a Newtonian fluid in a straight cylindrical tube with fully developed laminar flow.
cards.hint: Tube radius appears to the fourth power.

cards.front: What is hydraulic resistance in Poiseuille flow?
cards.back: R_h = ΔP/Q = 8ηL/(πr⁴).

cards.front: What is Stokes drag on a small sphere at low Reynolds number?
cards.back: F_d = 6πηrv, opposite motion relative to the fluid.

cards.front: What is the Reynolds number for pipe flow?
cards.back: Re = ρvD/η, where D is pipe diameter; it compares inertial and viscous effects.

cards.front: What is the ideal hydraulic press force relation?
cards.back: F1/A1 = F2/A2, neglecting height differences and losses.

cards.front: What is the ideal gas law?
cards.back: PV = nRT = Nk_BT. Use absolute temperature and absolute pressure.

cards.front: How are Celsius and Kelvin related?
cards.back: T_K = T_°C + 273.15. Temperature differences have the same numerical size in kelvins and Celsius degrees.

cards.front: What is heat transfer for a temperature change without a phase change?
cards.back: Q = mcΔT, if specific heat c is approximately constant.

cards.front: What is heat transfer during a phase change?
cards.back: Q = mL, where L is latent heat for the transition; temperature remains constant for an ideal pure substance at fixed pressure.

cards.front: What is linear thermal expansion for a small temperature change?
cards.back: ΔL = αL0ΔT, with linear expansion coefficient α.

cards.front: What is the first law of thermodynamics with work done by the system positive?
cards.back: ΔU = Q − W. Q is heat added to the system; W is work done by it.

cards.front: What is pressure-volume work at constant external pressure?
cards.back: W = P_ext ΔV for work done by the system; expansion gives positive W.

cards.front: What is work done by a gas in a reversible volume change?
cards.back: W = ∫P dV, the signed area under the pressure-volume curve.

cards.front: What is internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas?
cards.back: U = (3/2)nRT, ignoring nontranslational excitations.

cards.front: What is average translational kinetic energy per ideal-gas particle?
cards.back: K_avg = (3/2)k_BT.

cards.front: What is root-mean-square ideal-gas molecular speed?
cards.back: v_rms = √(3RT/M) = √(3k_BT/m), with molar mass M in kg/mol.

cards.front: What is heat-engine efficiency?
cards.back: e = W_net/Q_hot = 1 − Q_cold/Q_hot, using positive heat magnitudes.

cards.front: What is the maximum Carnot engine efficiency?
cards.back: e_C = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, with both temperatures in kelvins.

cards.front: What is entropy change for reversible heat transfer at constant temperature?
cards.back: ΔS = Q_rev/T.

cards.front: What is conductive heat-transfer rate through a flat slab?
cards.back: Q/t = kA(T_hot − T_cold)/L for steady one-dimensional conduction.

cards.front: What is net thermal radiation from a body to large surroundings?
cards.back: P_net = εσA(T⁴ − T_surroundings⁴), using absolute temperatures.

cards.front: What is Coulomb's law for force magnitude?
cards.back: F = k_e |q1q2|/r² for point charges. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

cards.front: How is electric field defined?
cards.back: E = F/q_test for a positive test charge. SI units: N/C or V/m.

cards.front: What is the electric field magnitude of a point charge?
cards.back: E = k_e |q|/r², outward for positive q and inward for negative q.

cards.front: What is electric potential due to a point charge?
cards.back: V = k_e q/r, relative to zero at infinity.

cards.front: What is electric potential energy of two point charges?
cards.back: U = k_e q1q2/r, relative to zero at infinity.

cards.front: How are electrical potential energy and potential difference related?
cards.back: ΔU = qΔV. Work done by the electric field is −qΔV.

cards.front: What is the field magnitude between ideal parallel plates?
cards.back: E = |ΔV|/d, neglecting edge effects; the field points toward lower potential.

cards.front: What is electric current?
cards.back: I = ΔQ/Δt for average current; SI unit: ampere, or coulomb per second.

cards.front: What is Ohm's law for an ohmic resistor?
cards.back: V = IR, with resistance constant under the stated conditions.

cards.front: How does resistance depend on a uniform wire's dimensions?
cards.back: R = ρ_e L/A, where ρ_e is electrical resistivity, L is length, and A is cross-sectional area.

cards.front: What is equivalent resistance in series?
cards.back: R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... . The same current passes through each series element.

cards.front: What is equivalent resistance in parallel?
cards.back: 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... . Each parallel branch has the same voltage.

cards.front: What is electrical power in a resistive element?
cards.back: P = IV = I²R = V²/R.

cards.front: What is Kirchhoff's junction rule?
cards.back: ΣI_in = ΣI_out, expressing charge conservation in a steady circuit.

cards.front: What is Kirchhoff's loop rule?
cards.back: The algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed circuit loop is zero in the usual lumped DC model.

cards.front: What is capacitance?
cards.back: C = Q/ΔV, using the magnitude of charge on one capacitor plate.

cards.front: What is capacitance of an ideal parallel-plate capacitor?
cards.back: C = κε0A/d, where κ is dielectric constant and edge effects are neglected.

What is equivalent capacitance in parallel?
What is equivalent capacitance in series?
What is the time constant of a simple RC circuit?
cards.back: τ = RC. It sets the exponential charging or discharging timescale.

cards.front: What is charge on a discharging ideal RC capacitor?
cards.back: Q(t) = Q0 e^(−t/RC), with no external source connected.

cards.front: What is magnetic force magnitude on a moving charge?
cards.back: F_B = |q|vB sin θ; θ is between velocity and field. The force is perpendicular to both.

cards.front: What is magnetic force magnitude on a straight current-carrying wire?
cards.back: F_B = ILB sin θ for a uniform field and straight wire segment of length L.

cards.front: What is the radius of circular motion of a charge perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field?
cards.back: r = mv/(|q|B), for nonrelativistic motion.

cards.front: What is magnetic flux through a flat loop in a uniform field?
cards.back: Φ_B = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between the field and the surface normal.

cards.front: What is Faraday's law for induced emf in N turns?
cards.back: ε = −N dΦ_B/dt. The minus sign expresses Lenz's law.

cards.front: What is the wave-speed relation?
cards.back: v = fλ, with frequency f and wavelength λ.

cards.front: How are period and frequency related?
cards.back: T = 1/f. Frequency is measured in hertz, or cycles per second.

cards.front: What is the period of an ideal mass-spring oscillator?
cards.back: T = 2π√(m/k), with negligible damping.

cards.front: What is the small-angle period of a simple pendulum?
cards.back: T = 2π√(L/g), for small oscillations and a pointlike bob on a massless string.

cards.front: What is wave intensity?
cards.back: I = P/A, power per area normal to propagation.

cards.front: What is intensity at distance r from an isotropic point source?
cards.back: I = P/(4πr²), neglecting absorption and reflections.

cards.front: What is sound intensity level in decibels?
cards.back: β = 10 log10(I/I0), commonly with I0 = 10^(−12) W/m² in air.

cards.front: What is the Doppler formula for sound when source and observer approach each other?
cards.back: f_observed = f_source (v + v_observer)/(v − v_source), with speeds relative to the medium and motion along their connecting line.

cards.front: What is refractive index?
cards.back: n = c/v, where v is light's phase speed in the medium and c is its vacuum speed.

cards.front: What is Snell's law?
cards.back: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. Angles are measured from the normal.

cards.front: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection?
cards.back: sin θ_c = n2/n1 when light travels from n1 to a lower index n2.

cards.front: What is the thin-lens or spherical-mirror equation in a real-is-positive convention?
cards.back: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i. Use consistent signs: real object and real image distances are positive; converging focal length is positive.

cards.front: What is transverse magnification in the usual thin-lens convention?
cards.back: m = h_i/h_o = −d_i/d_o. Negative m indicates an inverted image.

cards.front: What is optical power of a thin lens?
cards.back: P = 1/f with f in meters; unit: diopter. Converging lenses have positive power.

cards.front: What is photon energy?
cards.back: E = hf = hc/λ in vacuum.

cards.front: What is the photoelectric maximum kinetic energy equation?
cards.back: K_max = hf − φ when hf ≥ φ; φ is the material's work function.

cards.front: What is radioactive decay as a function of time?
cards.back: N(t) = N0 e^(−λt); half-life t_1/2 = ln 2/λ. Here λ is the decay constant, not wavelength.
